title: The Machine Caterpillar Feared Most
fullText: There is a machine so recognizable that its color alone became a trademark. Bright yellow, heavy steel. The kind of machine that moves mountains and levels forests and punches tunnels through solid rock. Caterpillar. For most of the 20th century, if you needed to build something big, there was really only one name on Earth that mattered. Caterpillar ran the planet. Their equipment was on every major construction site in every country that had the money to build. The United States Army used their machines. NASA used their machines. The largest mines in South America, the biggest dam projects in Africa, the highway systems spreading across Southeast Asia, yellow machines everywhere with that logo stamped across the engine hood. By the late 1970s, Caterpillar controlled roughly 35% of the entire global construction equipment market. They were the undisputed king of one of the most capitalintensive industries in human history. But in an office building in Osaka, Japan, the executives at a company called Kumatsu had taped something to their walls. A two-word phrase written in Japanese that translated roughly to this. Encircle Caterpillar. What followed was one of the most ruthless, methodical, and welldocumented corporate attacks in the history of American manufacturing. and Caterpillar almost did not survive it. To understand how a company this dominant almost disappeared, you need to go back to where it actually started, you need to go back to a California wheat field in 1894 and a man named Benjamin Hol who was furious about mud. Farming in the Sanwaqin Valley in the 1800s was not romantic work. The Delta soil was rich, but it was soft and it swallowed the wheels of harvesting machines whole. Steam-powered tractors that weighed 10 tons would sink up to their axles before they reached the end of a field. Hol spent years watching equipment fail in his fields. And he eventually decided he was going to solve the problem himself. His answer was to replace wheels with tracks, long, flat, continuous belts of metal that spread the machine's weight across a much larger surface area. So instead of sinking into soft ground, the machine floated across it. He tested his first continuous track tractor in November of 1894 on a field near Stockton, California. The machine worked. Holt's photographer reportedly watched it moving across the ground and said it looked like a caterpillar crawling across the earth. Hol liked the name and kept it. For the first few decades, caterpillars machines were mostly used in agriculture and logging. But the first world war changed everything. The British army took Holtz track concept, enclosed it in steel, put a cannon on top, and invented the tank. Suddenly, the entire world understood that tracked machines could move across terrain that would stop anything else. After the war, governments and private companies started spending enormous amounts of money on infrastructure, roads, dams, canals, airports, and every one of those projects needed earthmoving equipment. Caterpillar was right there, already making the best tracked machines in the world, ready to scale. By 1925, Halt Manufacturing had merged with a competitor called the CL Best Tractor Company, and the combined entity was officially renamed Caterpillar Tractor Company. They set up their headquarters in Peoria, Illinois, in the heart of American manufacturing country. And they started growing in a way that would not stop for the next five decades. World War II accelerated everything again. Caterpillar machines built roads across the Pacific for the United States military. They moved Earth on islands that had never been touched by modern equipment. Army Corps of Engineers reports from the Pacific theater described caterpillar bulldozers working around the clock, sometimes under fire. The machines became synonymous with American industrial might. When the war ended and the post-war construction boom began, Caterpillar was the automatic choice for every major project on the planet. The interstate highway system in America built through the 1950s and60s was carved out of the earth largely by Caterpillar machines, the Aswan Dam in Egypt, the TransCanada Highway, the expansion of ports across Western Europe. By the early 1970s, Caterpillar was posting annual revenues that put them among the largest manufacturers in the world. Their equipment had a reputation for being overbuilt, overpriced, and absolutely indestructible. Contractors who bought Caterpillar machines expected to run them for 30 years. The machines often obliged. Caterpillar's leadership during this period was confident in a way that in retrospect probably crossed the line into arrogance. Their market position felt permanent. They had the technology. They had the dealer network. They had the brand loyalty. The yellow machines had become so dominant in so many markets that most of Caterpillar's executives genuinely could not imagine a scenario in which someone took that position away from them. Then they met Kamatsu. Kamasu was not new. The company had been making mining machinery and industrial equipment in Japan since 1917. But for most of its existence, Kamatsu operated at a very different level than Caterpillar. They built decent machines for the Japanese domestic market and a few export markets in Asia. The equipment worked. It was not worldclass. The turning point was 1964. Caterpillar looking to expand its presence in Japan formed a joint venture with a Japanese company called Mitsubishi. The partnership was called Shin Caterpillar Mitsubishi and it was designed to give Caterpillar access to the Japanese construction boom that was underway ahead of the Tokyo Olympics. Kamasu's leadership watched this happen and understood immediately what it meant. Caterpillar, the most dominant construction equipment company on the planet, was now setting up manufacturing operations in Kumasu's home market. The yellow machines were coming to Japan. And if Kamasu could not compete with them at home, they could not compete with them anywhere. So Kamasu's president at the time, a man named Rioichi Kawawaii, did something unusual. He did not panic, and he did not ignore the threat. He declared war openly and deliberately. He launched what became known internally as the Maru Sea campaign. In Japanese, maru is a character placed around a letter to indicate encirclement. Maru C meant surround and destroy caterpillar. This was not a metaphor. Kawawaii wrote the strategy down. He shared it with his employees. The stated objective of Kamatsu from that moment forward was to erode Caterpillar's market share globally until the American company was no longer the dominant player in the industry. The strategy had three phases. First, Kamasu would close the quality gap. They would invest heavily in engineering and manufacturing processes until their machines were genuinely competitive with Caterpillar on performance. Second, they would undercut Caterpillar on price. Japanese manufacturing in the 1960s and '7s was becoming extraordinarily efficient, and Kamasu intended to use that efficiency to offer comparable machines at significantly lower prices. Third, they would attack Caterpillar in every international market where Caterpillar was strong, not just nibble at the edges. A direct, sustained assault. What happened over the next 15 years was one of the most successful corporate comeback stories in Japanese industrial history. Kamasu invested heavily in quality control programs. They brought in consultants. They sent engineers to study manufacturing processes in other industries. Their defect rates dropped dramatically. Their reliability ratings climbed. By the late 1970s, an independent study of construction equipment performance found that Kamatsu machines were operating at quality levels that were genuinely close to Caterpillars. Not identical, but close enough that price became the deciding factor for a growing number of buyers. And on price, Kumatsu had a serious advantage. Their manufacturing costs were lower, their labor costs were lower, and the Japanese government was actively supporting export oriented manufacturers through favorable financing arrangements. Kumatsu could offer machines in international markets at prices that Caterpillar struggled to match. By 1980, Kumatsu had become the second largest construction equipment manufacturer in the world. They had gone from a regional Japanese company that Caterpillar barely noticed to a genuine global competitor in less than two decades. And Caterpillar's market share, which had seemed untouchable just 10 years earlier, was starting to erode. Then the currency markets decided to make everything worse. In the early 1980s, the United States dollar began one of the most dramatic appreciation cycles in modern economic history. Between 1980 and 1985, the dollar rose in value against most major currencies by somewhere between 40 and 60%. That sounds like an abstract financial fact until you understand what it meant in practical terms for a company like Caterpillar. Caterpillar built almost everything in the United States. They paid their workers in dollars. They bought their steel and their components in dollars. And then they tried to sell their equipment to construction companies in Brazil, Australia, Saudi Arabia, and Germany. Companies that earned their money in currencies that were now worth dramatically less against the dollar. A contractor in West Germany who bought a Caterpillar bulldozer in 1979 paid a certain price in Deutsche marks. By 1984, to buy that same bulldozer, the contractor needed to spend roughly 60% more Deutsche marks than they had 5 years earlier. Not because Caterpillar raised their prices, simply because the dollar had become so much more expensive relative to European currencies. Meanwhile, Kamasu built their machines in Japan and paid their workers in yen. The yen appreciated, too, but less dramatically than the dollar. Kamasu machines got somewhat more expensive in international markets. Caterpillar machines got dramatically more expensive. The price gap between the two companies which had already been significant became enormous. Construction companies around the world that had always bought Caterpillar out of loyalty and habit started looking at the numbers and choosing Kamatsu. Not because the machines were better, not because Caterpillar had done anything wrong, simply because the economics had shifted so dramatically that sticking with Caterpillar felt impossible to justify. Caterpillar's international sales, which had been a pillar of their business, collapsed. Revenues that had been climbing steadily for decades, started falling. In 1982, Caterpillar reported a loss of $180 million. In 1983, the losses grew to $345 million. In 1984, another $428 million in losses. 3 years, nearly $1 billion gone for a company that had printed money for 50 years. This was genuinely existential. Caterpillar was burning through cash reserves that had taken decades to build. Their bond ratings were being downgraded. Analysts were openly questioning whether the company could survive. And it was not just the external pressure. Inside Caterpillar, things were falling apart in a different way. Caterpillar's relationship with its workers had been deteriorating for years. The company had a union workforce largely represented by the United Auto Workers, and the contract negotiations in the early 1980s turned ugly. In October of 1982, the UAW went on strike. The work stoppage lasted more than 200 days. 200 days during which Caterpillar's already struggling factories went mostly silent. The financial hit from the strike layered on top of the losses from the currency crisis and the Kamatsu competition was severe. Caterpillar laid off tens of thousands of workers across their facilities in Illinois. Towns that had built their entire economies around caterpillar employment were devastated. East Peoria, Morton, Pontiac, communities where generation after generation had worked. The Caterpillar lines suddenly faced unemployment rates that looked like the 1930s. Internally, the culture at Caterpillar was fracturing. A company that had operated for decades from a position of confident dominance now had no obvious answer to what was happening to it. The currency crisis was not something Caterpillar had caused. They could not fix the dollar. They could not force the Federal Reserve to change monetary policy. The competitive threat from Kamatsu was real and growing. The labor relations were poisoned and the losses kept coming. There were serious people inside and outside the company during this period who believed Caterpillar might not make it. Investment banks were modeling scenarios in which the company went into bankruptcy. The yellow machines, which had seemed like they would be on every construction site forever, suddenly looked fragile. What happened next inside Caterpillar is one of the most instructive examples of corporate self-reinvention in American business history. And it started with a man named Donald Fights who would eventually become Caterpillar's chief executive and a company that had to completely reimagine how it made things. The core problem Caterpillar faced was structural. Their factories had been designed and built in an era when American manufacturing could afford inefficiency because nobody else could compete. giant plants, complicated logistics, long production runs, enormous inventory stockpiles. The system worked when you had no competition. When Kamatsu appeared with leaner operations and lower costs, the inefficiency became a fatal vulnerability. In 1986, Caterpillar launched a program they called the plant with a future. It was not a modest adjustment. It was a complete redesign of how they manufactured equipment. The investment was approximately $1.5 billion across their facilities over roughly 6 years. The plant with a future restructured Caterpillar's factories around a concept called cellular manufacturing. Instead of a traditional assembly line where a machine traveled through a long sequence of specialized stations, each with its own team of workers, Caterpillar reorganized their production into smaller cells. Each cell was responsible for producing a complete component or subsystem. The workers in each cell understood the entire process, not just one specialized step. Flexibility went up, defect rates went down. Inventory requirements dropped dramatically because components could be produced closer to when they were actually needed. The results took time to materialize, but when they did, they were significant. Caterpillar's production costs fell substantially across their main product lines. The time required to manufacture certain machines was cut nearly in half. Quality metrics improved to the point where Caterpillar could credibly argue again that their machines were not just the most durable, but also among the most efficiently produced in the industry. Meanwhile, something was happening on Kumasu's side of the equation that the Maru C strategy had never anticipated. Kamasu in the 1980s began to suffer from a version of the same disease that had nearly killed Caterpillar. Success and the arrogance that sometimes follows it. Having achieved global scale and demonstrated they could compete with the industry leader, some of Kamatsu's leadership began to believe that the hard work was essentially done. They started diversifying into electronics, robotics, and other industries that were far outside their core competency. They made acquisitions that strained their balance sheet. The focused intensity of the Maru sea years gave way to something more scattered. And then in 1985, the Plaza Accord changed the currency mathematics again. The major economic powers agreed to intervene in currency markets to bring the dollar back down to more sustainable levels. Over the following 2 years, the dollar fell sharply against the yen. The price advantage that had given Kamasu such a devastating edge in international markets compressed significantly. Suddenly, Kamasu's machines were not so dramatically cheaper than Caterpillars. The foundation of their competitive strategy had shifted under their feet. Kamasu responded by raising their prices in international markets. construction companies that had switched to Kamatsu during the early8s because the economics demanded it now ran the numbers again and found that the gap had narrowed considerably. Some of them switched back. Caterpillar emerging from its brutal restructuring with leaner factories and a sharper focus on its core business was ready to compete in a way it had not been at the height of the crisis. The company that had nearly collapsed under the weight of currency losses, labor strife, and competitive pressure had used those years of pain to rebuild itself into something more resilient. The contrast between what the two companies did under pressure is the most instructive part of this story. Caterpillar, facing near death, forced itself to confront every structural inefficiency in its business. The factories were redesigned. The supply chain was restructured. The relationship with dealers was overhauled. The company that came out of the late 1980s was leaner and harder than the company that had entered the early part of the decade. Kamasu, achieving early success in their war against Caterpillar, dispersed their energy into businesses they did not understand well. The focused aggression of the Marui campaign dissipated into strategic drift. They did not lose catastrophically. Kamasu remained a significant global player. But the ambition of destroying Caterpillar, the explicit goal that had driven everything they did for two decades, was never achieved. By the early 1990s, Caterpillar had largely stabilized. Their market share, which had been declining through the early and mid80s, stopped falling and began to recover. Their financial results returned to profitability. The billion dollars in losses that had stunned investors and terrified employees became history. But the labor battles were not finished. In 1991 and again in 1994, Caterpillar and the United Auto Workers went through additional strikes with some of the confrontations during the early '90s becoming nationally significant stories about the state of American labor relations. The strikes were brutal on both sides, and the eventual resolution left scars in Peoria and the surrounding communities that took many years to fade. Through all of it, the company continued to invest in the operational improvements that the plant with a future had started. New generations of equipment were designed with both performance and manufacturing efficiency in mind. Caterpillar's engineering teams, competing again from a position of financial stability, pushed their product development forward in ways that had been impossible during the crisis years. The dealer network, which had been strained during the losses of the early8s, was rebuilt and restructured. Caterpillar's approach to its dealers was reformed into a more genuine partnership model, and the dealer network became one of the company's most significant competitive advantages. A contractor who bought a Caterpillar machine in a remote location knew that parts and service were available. That certainty had always been a differentiator and Caterpillar invested heavily to make sure it remained one. The 1990s also brought significant expansion of the global construction market. The economies of Southeast Asia were growing rapidly through the mid90s. China was beginning the infrastructure build that would eventually become the largest construction program in human history. Latin American countries were investing in roads, ports, and energy infrastructure. Every one of these expanding markets was an opportunity for a company that had survived its near-death experience and came out the other side ready to compete. Caterpillar positioned itself aggressively in these growing markets and won significant share. The yellow machines appeared on construction sites in Malaysia, Indonesia, and Thailand. They moved earth in the coal mines of Australia and the copper mines of Chile. The brand that had seemed vulnerable for a decade reasserted itself across the global industry. Kumasu continued to be a formidable competitor throughout all of this. The Japanese company never went away, never collapsed, never surrendered the global market position they had built during the Maru Sea years. They remained the number two construction equipment manufacturer in the world. But number two in an industry where Caterpillar had set the terms of competition is a very different thing from what Kauaii's original strategy had intended. The Maru Sea campaign had said in plain language destroy Caterpillar. What actually happened was that Kamasu became a permanent and serious global competitor and Caterpillar survived, restructured, and in important ways became a stronger company because of the pressure it faced. The attack did not destroy its target. It made its target harder to kill. The story does not end there and it does not end cleanly. In the years after the 1990s recovery, Caterpillar continued to grow in ways that would have seemed impossible during the darkest years of the early 80s. Their revenues climbed steadily through the 2000s into the tens of billions. They became not just a construction equipment company, but a full industrial enterprise with significant businesses in diesel engines, financial services, rail equipment, and energy systems. By 2012, Caterpillar's annual revenues exceeded $65 billion. The company that had reported nearly a billion dollars in losses over three consecutive years in the 1980s was posting revenues that made them one of the largest industrial companies on the planet. Kamasu also grew substantially during this period, expanding their global reach and continuing to invest in new technology. The two companies remained locked in competition across every major market in the world. And the rivalry that had started with Kauai's Marusi declaration never fully ended. It evolved into something more like the permanent tension between two giants who had been shaped by their conflict with each other. In recent years, both companies have been navigating a new wave of disruption that makes the currency crisis of the 1980s look almost simple by comparison. The construction equipment industry is in the middle of an electrification transition. Batterypowered excavators and bulldozers that do not emit diesel exhaust are moving from concept to reality. The software systems that manage modern construction sites are becoming as important as the physical machines themselves. Autonomous and semiautonomous equipment, machines that can operate with minimal human input in certain environments are no longer science fiction. Caterpillar has invested heavily in these transitions and so has Kumatsu. The competition between them has shifted terrain again, moving from the purely mechanical domain where both companies made their reputations into the software, battery technology, and autonomous systems domains where neither company has the same historical advantage. There is something almost fitting about that. The story of Caterpillar and Kamatsu has always been about what happens when the terms of competition change and a company either adapts or disappears. Caterpillar nearly disappeared in the 1980s because the terms of competition changed and it was too slow to respond. It survived because it eventually found the will to transform itself radically. Now those terms are changing again. The yellow machines still move Earth on every continent. The Caterpillar logo, that distinctive triangle with the Gothic lettering, still appears on equipment working in mines, building highways, pushing through jungle terrain to create paths for pipelines, scraping foundation cuts for the towers going up in cities that barely existed a generation ago. The brand has an endurance to it that the numbers in those early 1980s annual reports suggested it might not live to see. Kamasu still builds machines in Japan and in factories spread across Asia, Europe, and the Americas. The Maru strategy succeeded in creating a company genuinely capable of competing globally with the best in the world, even if it fell short of its stated ultimate objective. That is, depending on how you read it, either a failure or an extraordinary achievement. What is not in dispute is what the rivalry actually produced. two companies that pushed each other into becoming better at what they do. Manufacturing processes that under competitive pressure became leaner and more sophisticated products that because both sides had to keep improving to stay relevant became more durable and capable than either company would likely have built without the threat of the other. workers and engineers and designers at both companies who spent careers being challenged by the knowledge that somewhere in Osaka or somewhere in Poria, someone else was trying to build a machine that would make theirs obsolete. The machine Caterpillar feared most was Kamatsus. And the machine Kamatsu feared most was Caterpillars. That mutual fear sustained across six decades of genuine competition is the actual product this story generated. Trong hầu hết thế kỷ 20, nếu bạn cần xây dựng một thứ gì đó lớn lao, hãy có thực sự chỉ có một cái tên trên Trái đất quan trọng. Caterpillar điều hành hành tinh. Thiết bị của họ có mặt trên mọi công trường xây dựng lớn ở mọi quốc gia có tiền để xây dựng. Quân đội Hoa Kỳ đã sử dụng máy móc của họ. NASA đã sử dụng máy móc của họ. Những mỏ lớn nhất Nam Mỹ, những dự án đập nước lớn nhất châu Phi, đường cao tốc hệ thống trải rộng khắp Đông Nam Á, máy móc màu vàng ở khắp mọi nơi với logo đó được dán khắp mui xe động cơ. Vào cuối những năm 1970, Caterpillar kiểm soát khoảng 35% toàn bộ thiết bị xây dựng toàn cầu chợ. Họ là vị vua không thể tranh cãi của một trong những ngành sử dụng nhiều vốn nhất về con người lịch sử. Nhưng trong một tòa nhà văn phòng ở Osaka, Nhật Bản, các giám đốc điều hành của một công ty đã gọi Kumatsu đã dán thứ gì đó lên tường của họ. Và cuối cùng anh ấy quyết định sẽ tự mình giải quyết vấn đề. Trong vài thập kỷ đầu tiên, máy sâu bướm chủ yếu được sử dụng trong nông nghiệp và khai thác gỗ. Nhưng chiến tranh thế giới thứ nhất đã thay đổi mọi thứ. Các báo cáo của Công binh Lục quân từ mặt trận Thái Bình Dương mô tả các máy ủi bánh xích đang làm việc xung quanh đồng hồ, đôi khi dưới lửa.
